lessonTitle: Boiler and Burner Efficiency: Losses, Excess Air and NOx

blocks.text: A hospital boiler house burns 400 tonnes of natural gas a year. When the commissioning engineer trims the burner so that the flue gas oxygen falls from 8 % to 3 %, the annual gas bill drops by about 4 %, yet the same trim, if pushed to 0.5 % oxygen, makes the flame smoky and wastes fuel again. The boiler's efficiency is a balance of losses, and the air setting is its main lever.

blocks.markdown: A boiler's **thermal efficiency** is the useful heat delivered to the water or steam divided by the fuel energy supplied. We can calculate it directly as output over input, or indirectly by subtracting all the losses from 100 %. The indirect method is more useful for diagnosis because it shows where the energy goes. Throughout this unit efficiency is based on the lower heating value (LHV) of the fuel, so the latent heat of the water vapour in the flue gas is treated as a separate or excluded term.

blocks.caption: Each $L$ is a loss expressed as a fraction of the fuel energy input

blocks.title: Stack (flue gas) loss
blocks.text: The stack loss is the sensible heat carried away by the hot flue gas. For a flue gas mass $\dot m_{fg}$ (kg/s) with mean specific heat $c_{p,fg}$ (about 1.1 kJ/kg K) leaving at $T_{stack}$ when the combustion air enters at $T_a$, $L_{stack}=\dot m_{fg}c_{p,fg}(T_{stack}-T_a)/(\dot m_fLHV)$.

blocks.markdown: Other losses are smaller but real. **Radiation and convection loss** is heat from the hot casing and pipework to the boiler room, roughly constant in kW, so it becomes a larger fraction at low load. **Blowdown loss** is the heat in the water drained to control dissolved solids. **Unburnt loss** is the energy left in CO, soot or unburned hydrocarbons in the flue gas. The stack loss is normally the largest, typically 5 to 15 % of the fuel energy.

blocks.title: Boiler efficiency by the loss method
blocks.prompt: A gas boiler burns fuel with LHV 50 MJ/kg and stoichiometric air-fuel ratio 17.19 kg/kg at 15 % excess air. Flue gas leaves at 220 $^\circ$C and combustion air enters at 20 $^\circ$C. Use $c_{p,fg}=1.12$ kJ/kg K. Radiation loss is 1.5 % and blowdown loss 1.0 % of the fuel energy. Find the efficiency.

steps.text: Flue gas mass per kg of fuel: actual air plus the fuel itself.
Stack loss per kg of fuel.
Express as a percentage of the fuel energy.

blocks.answer: The boiler efficiency is 88.2 % (LHV basis), with the stack loss the largest at 9.3 %.

blocks.markdown: The air supply sets a trade-off. Too little air and some fuel cannot find oxygen: carbon monoxide, soot and unburned hydrocarbons appear and the unburnt loss rises steeply. Too much air and the flue gas mass grows, so the stack loss increases, and the flame cools. The best setting is the smallest excess air at which CO is still low, with a safety margin for variations in fuel, wind and load.

blocks.caption: Typical effect of excess air for natural gas; exact values depend on the fuel and the burner.

blocks.title: Cost of excess air
blocks.prompt: Take the boiler of the previous example (all other conditions unchanged) and raise the excess air to 40 %. Find the new efficiency and the loss of efficiency.
blocks.answer: Efficiency falls from 88.2 % to 86.3 %, a loss of 1.9 points, simply from 25 % more excess air. This is why oxygen trim controls pay for themselves.

blocks.markdown: **Nitrogen oxides** (NO and NO$_2$, together NO$_x$) are pollutants formed in flames. There are three routes. **Thermal NO$_x$** (the Zeldovich mechanism) forms when atmospheric N$_2$ and O$_2$ react at high temperature; its rate increases very steeply above about 1800 K. **Prompt NO$_x$** forms in the flame front from hydrocarbon radicals. **Fuel NO$_x$** forms from nitrogen bound in the fuel, important for coal and heavy oil. Conditions that raise NO$_x$ are high flame temperature, long residence time at that temperature, and plentiful oxygen.

blocks.title: Efficiency and NO$_x$ pull in different directions
blocks.text: Reducing excess air cuts the stack loss but also raises flame temperature slightly, which can raise thermal NO$_x$. Air preheating improves efficiency but increases flame temperature and NO$_x$. Practical designs use staged combustion, flue gas recirculation or low-NO$_x$ burners to lower peak temperature and oxygen in the hottest zone.

blocks.caption: Qualitative effects; magnitudes depend on the burner.

items: Efficiency by the indirect method is 100 % minus all losses; the stack loss is the largest.
Flue gas mass per kg fuel is $AFR(1+e)+1$ for complete combustion.
Excess air has an optimum: below it CO and soot rise, above it stack loss rises.
NO$_x$ rises with flame temperature, residence time and available oxygen.

blocks.title: Quote the basis
blocks.text: Boiler efficiencies are quoted on an LHV or on an HHV basis; for natural gas the HHV is about 10 % above the LHV, so the same boiler has a lower efficiency on an HHV basis. Always state which one you are using.

points: Boiler efficiency equals useful output divided by fuel energy, or 100 % minus the stack, radiation, blowdown and unburnt losses.
Stack loss $=\dot m_{fg}c_p(T_{stack}-T_a)/(\dot m_fLHV)$ and grows with excess air and stack temperature.
Excess air trades unburnt loss at low air against stack loss at high air; the optimum is the smallest air that gives clean combustion.
NO$_x$ increases with high flame temperature, long residence time and abundant oxygen.

questions.stem: A fuel oil boiler produces 22 kg of flue gas per kg of fuel (LHV 44 MJ/kg). The flue gas leaves at 260 degrees Celsius, the combustion air enters at 25 degrees Celsius and the mean specific heat of the flue gas is 1.10 kJ/kg K. Find the stack loss as a percentage of the fuel LHV.
questions.explanation: The sensible heat per kg of fuel is 22 x 1.10 x (260 - 25) = 5687 kJ. Dividing by the LHV of 44 000 kJ/kg gives a stack loss of 12.9 %. This is the largest loss in most boilers.

questions.stem: A boiler burns 0.80 kg/s of oil with LHV 42 MJ/kg and delivers 28.2 MW of useful heat to steam. Find the thermal efficiency on an LHV basis in percent.
questions.explanation: The fuel energy rate is 0.80 x 42 = 33.6 MW. The efficiency is 28.2/33.6 = 0.8393, or 83.9 %. The remaining 5.4 MW is lost to the flue gas, casing and other losses.

questions.stem: An economiser lowers the flue gas temperature from 260 degrees Celsius to 170 degrees Celsius for the boiler with 22 kg flue gas per kg oil, LHV 44 MJ/kg, specific heat 1.10 kJ/kg K and air inlet at 25 degrees Celsius. By how many percentage points does the boiler efficiency improve, assuming other losses are unchanged?
questions.explanation: The stack loss falls from 12.93 % to 22 x 1.10 x (170 - 25)/44 000 = 7.98 %. The difference is 4.95 percentage points, which is also the gain in efficiency because the other losses are fixed.

questions.stem: A gas burner has a stoichiometric air-fuel ratio of 16.0 kg/kg and fuel LHV of 46 MJ/kg. The flue gas leaves 180 K above the air inlet temperature with specific heat 1.10 kJ/kg K. By how many percentage points does the stack loss increase when the excess air is raised from 10 % to 40 %? Take the flue gas mass as AFR(1+e)+1 per kg of fuel.
questions.explanation: At 10 % excess air the flue mass is 16.0 x 1.10 + 1 = 18.6 kg/kg, giving 18.6 x 1.10 x 180/46 000 = 8.01 %. At 40 % it is 16.0 x 1.40 + 1 = 23.4 kg/kg, giving 10.07 %. The increase is 2.07 percentage points.

questions.stem: Why is a burner not normally set to supply exactly the stoichiometric amount of air (zero excess air)?

options.text: Imperfect mixing and fluctuations would leave some fuel unburned, giving CO and soot, so a small excess of air is needed
Because stoichiometric air makes the flue gas cooler and increases the stack loss
Because the burner would produce more NO$_x$ at the stoichiometric point than at any other
Because air is cheaper than fuel

questions.correctOptionText: Imperfect mixing and fluctuations would leave some fuel unburned, giving CO and soot, so a small excess of air is needed

distractorRationale.b: Zero excess air gives the lowest flue gas mass and so the lowest stack loss, not a higher one.
distractorRationale.c: NO$_x$ depends on temperature and oxygen; the main reason for excess air is complete combustion.
distractorRationale.d: The reason is combustion completeness; the cost of air is negligible compared with the fuel waste caused by high excess air.

questions.explanation: Real burners never mix fuel and air perfectly, so a stoichiometric supply would leave some regions fuel-rich, producing CO, soot and unburned fuel. A small safety margin of air gives clean combustion at slightly higher stack loss.

questions.stem: A boiler's flue gas oxygen is trimmed from 7 % to 3 % while the stack temperature and everything else stay the same. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Stack loss falls because less flue gas is produced per kg of fuel, improving efficiency if CO stays low
Stack loss rises because more fuel is needed
Efficiency does not change because the fuel energy is the same
Efficiency falls because the unburnt loss is always larger at low oxygen

questions.correctOptionText: Stack loss falls because less flue gas is produced per kg of fuel, improving efficiency if CO stays low

distractorRationale.b: Less excess air means less flue gas to heat; the fuel burned is the same.
distractorRationale.c: The mass of hot flue gas leaving changes, so stack loss changes.
distractorRationale.d: Unburnt loss increases only when oxygen falls too far; at 3 % it is normally small.

questions.explanation: Reducing the oxygen means less excess air, a smaller flue gas mass, and so a lower sensible heat loss. The gain is lost only if the air is reduced so far that CO and soot form, which raises the unburnt loss.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes is most likely to INCREASE thermal NO$_x$ formation in a gas burner, all else equal?

options.text: Preheating the combustion air, which raises the peak flame temperature
Recirculating cooled flue gas into the combustion air
Staging the air so that the first zone is fuel-rich
Shortening the residence time at high temperature

questions.correctOptionText: Preheating the combustion air, which raises the peak flame temperature

distractorRationale.b: FGR dilutes the oxygen and lowers peak temperature, reducing NO$_x$.
distractorRationale.c: Staging lowers peak temperature and oxygen in the hot zone, reducing NO$_x$.
distractorRationale.d: Less time at high temperature gives less NO formation.

questions.explanation: Thermal NO$_x$ increases steeply with temperature, so anything that raises peak flame temperature raises NO$_x$. Air preheat improves efficiency but must be balanced with NO$_x$ controls.

questions.stem: Which combination of conditions favours the highest thermal NO$_x$ formation?

options.text: High flame temperature, long residence time in the hot zone and plentiful oxygen
Low flame temperature, long residence time and plentiful oxygen
High flame temperature, short residence time and no oxygen
Low flame temperature, short residence time and excess fuel

questions.correctOptionText: High flame temperature, long residence time in the hot zone and plentiful oxygen

distractorRationale.b: At low temperature the reaction is too slow, whatever the oxygen supply.
distractorRationale.c: Without oxygen, NO cannot form, and the short time further limits it.
distractorRationale.d: These conditions all suppress thermal NO$_x$.

questions.explanation: The Zeldovich reactions need nitrogen and oxygen atoms, which appear only at high temperature, and they need time to proceed. All three of high temperature, long time and available oxygen are therefore necessary for large NO$_x$ formation.

questions.stem: Explain, with reference to the stack loss and the unburnt loss, why there is an optimum excess air for a boiler, and sketch how efficiency varies with the excess air.
markingGuide: At low excess air the unburnt loss (CO, soot) increases sharply because of incomplete combustion
At high excess air the flue gas mass increases so the stack loss increases (flue gas mass $=AFR(1+e)+1$)
Efficiency is maximum at the minimum of the sum of these two losses, at a small excess air (about 5 to 15 % for gas)
Mentions the flame temperature reduction at high excess air
Mentions safety margin for fuel variation and load changes, or oxygen trim control
questions.explanation: The two losses move in opposite directions as the air is changed, so their sum has a minimum. Operators keep a margin on the lean side of that minimum so that disturbances do not push the burner into CO formation.

questions.stem: Describe the main mechanisms by which NO$_x$ forms in a flame and explain two measures that reduce thermal NO$_x$ together with their effect on boiler efficiency.
markingGuide: Thermal NO$_x$: Zeldovich mechanism, strongly temperature dependent above about 1800 K, needs O and N atoms and time
Prompt NO$_x$ from hydrocarbon radicals in the flame front, and fuel NO$_x$ from nitrogen in the fuel
Flue gas recirculation lowers flame temperature and oxygen concentration, with a small efficiency penalty due to higher fan power
Staged combustion or low-NO$_x$ burners lower the peak temperature and oxygen in the hottest zone
Notes trade-off: lower temperature may increase CO or reduce flame stability, and air preheat improves efficiency but raises NO$_x$
questions.explanation: NO$_x$ formation is governed by temperature, time and oxygen, so reduction measures cool the flame or limit oxygen. Each carries some cost in efficiency or stability, which has to be balanced in the burner design.
